food.text: In 1584, the Danzig merchant Martin Gruneweg travelled through Kyiv and noted how widely borshch was eaten. According to him, it was cooked in almost every household and consumed daily as both food and drink.

Cold sour soups were common across all social ranks in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the later Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, from the nobility to the peasants. Cold beet soup is historically tied to this tradition and survives in several countries today.
In 17th-century Russia, cuisine split along economic lines. The rich ate meat and delicacies such as caviar, while the poor ate the simplest dishes. New foods also appeared as new lands were annexed.

Ivan Vyshenskyi, an Orthodox polemicist from Galicia, described borshch as a typical peasant food. This is another early mention of the dish in Ukrainian lands, alongside Gruneweg's account from 1584.

In the 18th century, after parts of Ukraine joined the Russian Empire, borshch became popular at the imperial court in Saint Petersburg. Ivan Kotliarevsky's Eneida also mentioned it, alongside halushky.

The word for soup was not known in Belarus until the 18th century, when the nobility borrowed it from German. Before that, most traditional soups were called polivka, unless named for their main vegetable, such as kapusta for cabbage soup.
Since wheat does not grow well in Belarus's cold, wet climate, Belarusians favoured sour rye bread. Their most traditional hard drink, harelka, was a vodka distilled mainly from rye malt.
Cold meat rolls, salcesons and balerons were borrowed from Italian cuisine by the Belarusian nobility in the 16th century. By the 19th century they were common to all of society.

At the end of the 18th century, Paul Tremo, head chef to King Stanisław August Poniatowski, recorded one of the earliest known recipes for chłodnik in Warsaw. Around the same time, the military doctor Jan Drozdowski described a noble household's version that included crayfish tails and sour cream.
Tula gingerbread is known as early as 1685. Confectioners made it using gingerbread molds hand carved into planks of wood taken from local birch and pear trees.
Jan Drozdowski wrote that he first tasted a cold soup prepared by a local woman in Biała-Radziwiłłowska, who called it chołodec. He noted it was also called chłodnik, and among common people boćwina.

art.text: Russian architecture developed unique tent-like churches in the 16th century, and the onion dome became a distinctive feature of Russian architecture. Italian architects such as Aristotle Fioravanti had earlier brought Renaissance trends into Russia.

The Kremlin walls were redone between 1485 and 1516 in brick, replacing limestone walls that had fallen into disrepair. They were a derivation of a then-outdated style of Italian fortification engineering.

Under Peter the Great and Elizabeth of Russia, Russian Baroque emerged in Saint Petersburg and Moscow. The style appeared in the Russian Tsardom and Empire during the late 17th and early 18th centuries.

Russian church architecture developed distinctive forms in the 16th century, when unique tent-like churches and the onion dome appeared. In the 17th century the "fiery style" of ornamentation flourished in Moscow and Yaroslavl, paving the way for the Naryshkin baroque of the 1690s.

Before the 17th century, the personal, innovative traditions of Western European religious art were largely lacking in Russia. In the 17th century Russian icon painting became strongly influenced by religious paintings and engravings from both Protestant and Catholic Europe.

The Italian architect Aloisio the New built the cathedral of St Michael in the Kremlin between 1505 and 1509. He incorporated several Italianate details in the facade and decoration but maintained the traditional plan prototype.

Since tents were banned, Muscovite architects replaced them with rows of corbel arches called kokoshniks, which became a hallmark of the 17th-century Moscow style. An early example is the Kazan Cathedral on Red Square, built in 1633 to 1636.

The Russian Academy of Arts was created in 1757 to give Russian artists an international role and status. Notable portrait painters from the academy include Ivan Argunov, Fyodor Rokotov, Dmitry Levitzky and Vladimir Borovikovsky.
Étienne Maurice Falconet created the monumental Bronze Horseman, an equestrian monument in Saint Petersburg, for Catherine the Great. He worked on it from 1768 to 1782.
Pietro Antonio Solari, another Italian, added several parts to the Kremlin. These included the four entrance towers, the Arsenal tower, and the Kremlin wall facing the Red Square.

The Naryshkin Baroque included the multi-domed Assumption Church on Pokrovka Street in Moscow, built 1696 to 1699 and demolished in 1929. Its architect also carried out the red and white reconstruction of the Novodevichy Convent and the Donskoy Monastery.

Four churches were built in the Stroganov Baroque, a conventional form of Moscow Baroque. They were the Stroganov and Smolensk churches in Nizhny Novgorod, the Presentation Cathedral in Solvychegodsk, and the Church of Our Lady of Kazan in Ustyuzhna.

The village of Fedoskino, near Moscow on the banks of the Ucha River, has practiced lacquer miniature painting on papier-mâché since 1795. It is the oldest of the four Russian lacquer art centers and stands apart in using oil paints rather than egg tempera.

war.text: Beginning in 1644, the Russian town of Pustozersk, north of the Arctic Circle, was frequently attacked by Samoyedic peoples. The town stood in the lower reaches of the Pechora River, on the far northern edge of the Russian state.
Between 1500 and 1700 the Crimean Khanate exported about 2 million slaves from Russia and Ukraine to the Ottoman Empire and the Middle East. This trade lasted until the late 18th century.

From 1609 to 1618, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Tsardom of Russia fought a war that grew out of Russia's Time of Troubles. Polish forces won many early victories, such as the 1610 Battle of Klushino, and in 1610 Polish units entered Moscow.

In 1569 the Ottoman Sultan Selim II sent an expedition to Astrakhan to push the Russians out of the lower Volga. It ended in disaster: the army could not take Astrakhan and almost completely perished in the steppes, while a storm wrecked the Ottoman fleet in the Sea of Azov.

When Sweden invaded Russia in 1707, Peter avoided battle and used scorched earth tactics. The winter of 1708/1709 was one of the coldest of a mini ice age, and on 8 July 1709 the Swedes were decisively beaten at the Battle of Poltava.

From 1550 to 1700, Russia grew by an average of 35,000 square kilometres per year. This period included wars with the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire, as well as the Russian conquest of Siberia.

Pustozersk was the most distant northern outpost of Muscovy and the first Russian settlement on the Pechora. It was supposed to play the role of a military fort on the northern borders of the Russian state.

Charles XII of Sweden, called Carolus Rex in the article, invaded Russia in 1707, and Peter pursued scorched earth tactics. After the cold winter of 1708 to 1709, the Swedes were decisively defeated at the Battle of Poltava on July 8, 1709.

In September 1610 the Seven Boyars elected Prince Władysław, the son of King Sigismund III Vasa, as tsar of Russia. Earlier, on 24 February, Sigismund had written that he would agree to this, but only once Moscow was at peace.

In July 1677 the Ottoman sultan sent an army of 45,000 men under Ibrahim Pasha to Chyhyryn. After Russian and Ukrainian forces relieved the town on 5 September, the Ottoman army had lost 20,000 men. Ibrahim was imprisoned on his return to Constantinople, and Crimean Khan Selim I Giray lost his throne.

Hetman Ivan Mazepa allied with Charles XII of Sweden in 1708. The Great Frost of 1709 greatly weakened the Swedish army, and after the Battle of Poltava later that year the power of the Cossack Hetmanate diminished.

Bohdan Khmelnytsky led the Cossacks to victory in an uprising against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth between 1648 and 1654. In 1648–1649 the Cossacks under his leadership massacred tens of thousands of Poles and Jews, and handed more over as slaves (yasir) to his Crimean Tatar allies. The massacres continued under his rule until at least 1652 and possibly caused hundreds of thousands of deaths, with the goal of eradicating non-Orthodox Ruthenian populations. In 1654 he concluded the Treaty of Pereiaslav with the Russian Tsar, placing Ukraine under Russian protection.
The Crimean Khanate, an Ottoman vassal, kept expanding against the Tsardom of Russia and burned down Moscow in 1571. It was defeated the following year at the Battle of Molodi in 1572.

To reach Chyhyryn, Samoilovich and Romodanovsky's army had to cross the Sula river. A skirmish on 26–27 August removed Ottoman observation posts, letting the rest cross under artillery fire, and Turkish attempts to drop back into the river at the first crossing detachment under Major-General Shepelev were repulsed. On 28 August Russian and Ukrainian cavalry attacked and overwhelmed the Turkish-Tatar camp, inflicting heavy casualties.

In January 1769 a Turkish-Tatar army of 70 thousand under Crimean Khan Qırım Giray invaded central Ukraine. Its troops ravaged New Serbia and took many slaves, but the raid was repulsed by the garrison of the Fortress of St. Elizabeth.

literature.text: In 1574 the printer Ivan Fedorov, who had settled in Lviv in 1572, printed the Apostol and a Primer. These two books mark the conventional starting point of Ukrainian printing. The Primer was the first known printed schoolbook in the Eastern Slavic lands.

In 1574 the printer Ivan Fedorov, who had settled in Lviv in 1572, printed two books that mark the conventional start of Ukrainian printing. One was the Apostol, and the other was a Primer, the first known printed schoolbook in the Eastern Slavic lands.

Peter the Great's reign at the start of the 18th century set off a series of modernizing changes in Russian literature. Writers then debated the function and form of literature as it related to the Russian language. These debates set a stylistic precedent for the sharper, more topical and controversial work of the late 18th century.

Alexander Nikolayevich Radishchev shocked the Russian public with his depictions of the socio-economic condition of the serfs. Empress Catherine II condemned this portrayal and forced him into exile in Siberia.

Ivan Fedorov later moved to Ostroh. There, under the patronage of Prince Vasyl-Kostiantyn Ostrozky, he printed the celebrated Ostrog Bible in 1581, the first complete printed Bible in Church Slavonic.

After moving to Ostroh, Ivan Fedorov worked under the patronage of Prince Vasyl-Kostiantyn Ostrozky. In 1581 he printed the celebrated Ostrog Bible there. It was the first complete printed Bible in Church Slavonic.

In 1892 Ivan Franko presented his own work on Ukrainian literature of the 16th to 18th centuries, in opposition to claims that its future lay only in union with Russia. He argued that the chronology of Ukrainian literary history should start not from 1798 but from the Medieval era.

The press of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra was founded in 1615 under Yelisey Pletenetsky and became the largest in the Cossack Hetmanate. In 1616 it produced its first book, the Book of Hours, the first book printed in Kyiv.

After Fedorov died in 1583, his Lviv press was acquired by the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood. Its printing house became one of the most influential publishing centres in Eastern Europe in the 17th century, producing liturgical, polemical and educational books.

Ukrainian presses at places such as Pochaiv Lavra and Chernihiv printed more than liturgical books. They also produced theology, polemics, history and grammar, including Meletius Smotrytsky's influential Slavonic Grammar in 1619.

In 1880 Nikolai Petrov, a professor at the Kiev Theological Academy, presented an overview of 18th century Ukrainian Baroque drama. His work sparked a discussion that was limited by Russian censorship. It was among the first academic works on the history of Ukrainian literature.

Ippolit Bogdanovich's narrative poem Dushenka, from 1778, is a rare sample of the Rococo style in Russia. It is erotic light poetry, standing apart from the more political and controversial works of Catherine the Great's reign.

The English visitors Giles Fletcher and Samuel Collins wrote about Russia, in Of the Russe Common Wealth (1591) and The Present State of Russia (1668). Both used the name Russia, although much of Europe called the country Moscovia or Muscovy.

The Harvard Library of Early Ukrainian Literature was launched by Omeljan Pritsak in 1987 to publish the main Ukrainian literary works up to the end of the eighteenth century. Its first volume, from 1989, was the Collected Works of Meletius Smotrytsky.

literature.text: Vasily Levshin's Newest Voyage, published in 1784, is described as the first Russian "flight" to the Moon. It was an early utopia written in the form of an imaginary voyage, part of a wave of Russian speculative fiction in the 18th century.

science.text: Peter the Great established the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences in 1724, with guidance from the German thinker Gottfried Leibniz. It later grew into the Russian Academy of Sciences. The majority of Russian scientific research in the 18th century was done by its members.

From its founding, the St. Petersburg academy relied on foreign scholars as professors. Among the mathematicians invited were Leonhard Euler, Daniel Bernoulli and Christian Goldbach. The list also included a botanist, an embryologist, a physicist, and an astronomer and geographer.

Academy scientists led or joined expeditions to explore remote parts of the Russian Empire. These included Vitus Bering's Second Kamchatka Expedition of 1733 to 1743 and the expeditions of Peter Simon Pallas to Siberia. The work produced an atlas of Russia and research in astronomy, geography, fauna and flora.

For the 1769 transit of Venus, the academy organised expeditions to observe it from eight locations across the Russian Empire. Such expeditions were led or actively joined by Academy scientists. They fed research in astronomy and geography.

From 1750 to 1777, the academy published 20 volumes of its academic journal, Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitanae. It gave the work of the academy's scholars a wide audience.

Science and technology in Russia developed rapidly after Peter the Great founded the Russian Academy of Sciences and Saint Petersburg State University. The polymath Mikhail Lomonosov founded Moscow State University, helping establish a strong native tradition in learning and innovation.

Peter the Great, following Leibniz's instructions, offered the philosopher Christian Wolff the Vice-Presidency of the academy in the early 1720s. Wolff declined the position. He did invite western scholars to work at the academy to improve higher education in the Russian Empire, as Leibniz's letters had outlined.
The academy gained its first clear set of goals from the 1747 Charter. Until then it had been guided mainly by the foreign scholars who filled its professorships.

The academy's foreign recruits included the botanist Johann Georg Gmelin, the embryologist Caspar Friedrich Wolff and the physicist Georg Wolfgang Kraft. Joseph-Nicolas Delisle came as an astronomer and geographer. Even the English Astronomer Royal Nevil Maskelyne is listed among those invited.

Nicholas Bernoulli (1695 to 1726) and Daniel Bernoulli (1700 to 1782) were both mathematicians invited to the St. Petersburg academy. Nicholas died in 1726, only two years after the academy's founding in 1724. The article gives no cause of death.

politics.text: Ivan IV was the first Russian monarch to be crowned as tsar, in 1547. Between 1550 and 1700, the Russian state grew by an average of 35,000 square kilometres per year.
Peter the Great took power in 1689 and transformed the Tsardom into an empire. After victory over Sweden in the Great Northern War, he proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721.

Catherine the Great waged two wars against the decaying Ottoman Empire, in 1768 to 1774 and 1787 to 1792, and pushed Russia's southern boundary to the Black Sea. Russia also annexed Crimea in 1783 and created the Black Sea fleet.

Peter the Great made the nobility wear Western European clothing and shave off their beards, which the boyars protested bitterly. He also banned arranged marriages among the nobility and brought the Orthodox Church under state control.

After a 1648 Cossack rebellion against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky agreed to the Treaty of Pereyaslav in January 1654. The treaty precipitated the Russo-Polish War of 1654 to 1667, and left-bank Ukraine was incorporated into Russia in 1667 under the Treaty of Andrusovo.

The partition of Poland in the 18th century gave Russia, for the first time in its history, land with a large Jewish population. This land was designated the Pale of Settlement, from which Jews were forbidden to migrate into the interior of Russia. In 1772 Catherine II forced the Jews of the Pale of Settlement to stay in their shtetls and forbade them from returning to the towns they had occupied before the partition. The Pale was officialized in 1791 with the purpose of ridding Moscow of Jews.
Peter the Great's administrative reforms had a lasting impact on Russia. He created a Governing Senate in 1711, the Collegium in 1717 and the Table of Ranks in 1722.

The Treaty of Nystad in 1721 ended the Great Northern War. Sweden ceded large parts of Karelia, and all of Ingria, Estonia and Livonia to Russia, which formalized the control of Saint Petersburg, the capital since 1712.

In 1783 Heraclius II of Kartli-Kakheti signed the Treaty of Georgievsk with Catherine, agreeing to forswear allegiance to any state except Russia in return for Russian protection. When another Russo-Turkish War broke out in 1787, the Russians withdrew their troops and left his kingdom unprotected. In 1795 the Persian shah Agha Mohammad Khan ordered Heraclius to break off relations with Russia or face invasion; Heraclius ignored it, counting on Russian help that did not arrive. Agha Mohammad Khan captured Tbilisi and burned it to the ground, and the Persians sacked the city, leaving 20,000 dead.
In 1775 Catherine the Great liquidated the Zaporozhian Sich. On the former Cossack lands the Novorossiya Governorate was created, with new cities such as Kherson in 1778 and Odessa in 1794.

In 1720 a ukase of Peter the Great forbade the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra and Chernihiv presses from printing any books except those that fully matched Russian editions in language and content. The decree effectively ended independent Ukrainian-language ecclesiastical and scholarly printing under Russian rule.

The Treaty of Perpetual Peace, signed in 1686, placed eastern Ukraine under Russian rule and required 146,000 rubles to be paid to Poland as compensation. The Polish-Lithuanian Sejm did not ratify it until 1710, and its legitimacy has been disputed.

philosophy.text: Russian philosophy of the 18th century is associated with thinkers such as Feofan Prokopovich, Stefan Yavorsky, Mikhail Lomonosov and Grigory Skovoroda. Russian Martinists and so-called Inner Christians also count among its important figures.

In 1653 Patriarch Nikon's reform led the Old Believers to break away from the Russian Orthodox Church, an event called the Raskol. They and the movement known as Spiritual Christianity challenged the Church's monopoly and put forward stances of freedom of conscience.

In 1596 the Union of Brest formed the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, meant to unify Eastern Orthodox and Catholic believers. It became traditionally the second largest group of believers after the Orthodox churches.

Several central works of 18th-century Russian philosophy carried plain, searching titles. They include Vasily Tatishchev's A Conversation of Two Friends, Andrei Bolotov's Children's Philosophy, and Alexander Radishchev's About Man, His Mortality and Immortality.

The Rtishchevsky School, also called the Rtishchevsky Brotherhood, was the first educational institution in Russia. It began as a court circle under Alexei Mikhailovich and taught on the model of European higher education. It operated in Moscow from 1648 at the Andreevsky Monastery.

In the 18th century a new teaching of Judaism, Hasidism, originated and became established in the Ukrainian lands. Ashkenazi Jewish presence there had already grown significantly from the 13th century.

The Russian Orthodox Church never forbade personal religious experience or speculative mysticism. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the thought of Jakob Böhme was popular in Orthodox seminaries, strengthening Gnostic elements that had been embedded in Orthodox Christianity since the sixth century.

In 1686 the Metropolitanate of Kyiv was annexed by the Moscow Patriarchate through a synodal letter of the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, Dionysius IV. This placed the Kyiv church under Moscow's authority.

Uniate Catholicism, officially founded in 1596 under Polish rule, eventually declined in the Ukrainian lands under Tsarist control. The source ties this to the domination of Little Russia by Great Russia from 1721.

Followers of a modern Ukrainian faith consider Podolia the heart of an ancient civilisation. They say the Bolokhivsky princes defended the ancient Slavic religion there longest and most strenuously, ostensibly as late as 1620. The Zbruch Idol, representing Svetovid, was found in the same place.

culture.text: Peter the Great suppressed numerous rebellions with considerable bloodshed, and then embarked on an incognito tour of Western Europe, which impressed him. Afterward he began requiring the nobility to wear Western European clothing and shave off their beards, and the boyars protested bitterly. He also banned arranged marriages among the nobility.

The kokoshnik was a women's headdress worn primarily in the northern regions of Russia from the 16th to 19th centuries. Poorer people in Old Russia and the northern regions commonly wore lapti and similar shoes.

In the mid-17th century, changes in liturgy and practice instituted by Patriarch Nikon split the Russian Orthodox Church. The persecuted Old Believers continued the traditional stylization of icons, while the State Church began to accept icons that mixed Russian stylization with Western European realism.

The ushanka's design was influenced in the 17th century by a hat with earflaps called the treukh, worn in central and northern Russia. Valenki, traditional Russian shoes, come from 18th-century designs that originally came from Asian nomads of the Great steppe.
